# agent-workflows

A Claude Code plugin that carries one piece of work from a remark in a session to merged:
file the issue, claim it, do the work, judge what state it actually reached, open the
change request, land it. Fourteen skills, each stopping for a person. Nothing auto-runs
the next.

## Requirements

- [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs) with plugin support
- `gh` or `glab`, installed and authenticated. Every step that touches an issue or a change
  request goes through one of them, and the skills derive which from `git remote`
- `rsvg-convert` — only for `gen-readme`, which renders diagrams

## Install

    /plugin marketplace add dogkeeper886/agent-workflows
    /plugin install agent-workflows@agent-workflows

Then ask for what you want in your own words, or invoke a skill by name:

    /agent-workflows:file-issue the parser drops trailing commas
    /agent-workflows:take-issue 42

The namespaced form always reaches the installed unit. A bare `/file-issue` reaches a local
copy of that name when your project has one.

## How it works

![The spine: six skills from a remark to merged](docs/diagrams/png/01-the-spine.png)

The issue is the portal. When you say *"merge it"* you say nothing about the issue, the
branch, or what was discussed three days ago — `land-pr` walks back from the change request
to the issue to the branch. Without that join every step would need you to carry context
forward, which is the drift this exists to remove.

**`review-work` is the reason the chain is worth having.** A step that always advanced
would be a formality. Four of its five outcomes send the work somewhere other than a change
request, and those four — half done, stuck, two tasks under one number, never started — are
the states that otherwise go unrecorded.

**The toolkit keeps no state of its own.** No story file, no plan file, no index. The
issue, its labels, the branch and the change request live on the platform, which is the one
place both a person and an agent can read.

## Not all work ends in a diff

![The fork after do-task: a diff goes to a change request, evidence closes the issue](docs/diagrams/png/02-diff-or-evidence.png)

A cert rotated, a cluster restarted, data migrated: the act is the deliverable. `do-task`
performs it, records the command, its output and the before-and-after state on the issue,
and closes it. No branch is cut, and no change request is ever opened — which is also why
`take-issue` cuts a branch only when a diff is coming.

`file-issue` carries the same fork upstream, with a template per kind:
[bug](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/bug.md) ·
[task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/task.md) ·
[docs](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/docs.md) ·
[environment](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/environment.md) ·
[operation](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/operation.md).

## The skills

| Skill | What it does |
|---|---|
| [file-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md) | Turns something said in a session into an issue a cold agent can act on, and copies the session log beside it |
| [take-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/take-issue/SKILL.md) | Reads the issue whole, refuses it back when it cannot be started, or claims it and stops before any work |
| [do-task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/do-task/SKILL.md) | Writes and commits the change, or performs the act and captures the evidence |
| [review-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-work/SKILL.md) | Judges which of five states the work reached, and routes it there |
| [open-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/open-pr/SKILL.md) | Pushes the branch and opens the change request, linked so the issue closes on merge |
| [land-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/land-pr/SKILL.md) | Merges at a pinned SHA after a person answers whether they reviewed and tested it, then cleans up |
| [plan-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/plan-work/SKILL.md) | Splits work too large for one issue, grouped with whatever the platform already provides |
| [gen-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/gen-readme/SKILL.md) | Writes a README from the code, with one rendered diagram per key point |
| [review-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-readme/SKILL.md) | Gates a README on three counts: useful to a newcomer, true to the code, and readable |
| [reviewing-artifacts](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-artifacts/SKILL.md) | Gates the files an agent reads — skills, commands, rules. Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT |
| [reviewing-phrasing](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-phrasing/SKILL.md) | Reviews the words of a human-read document, greping the mechanical tells first |
| [reviewing-typography](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-typography/SKILL.md) | Reviews how such a document looks, the way a UI designer would |
| [reporting-outcomes](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reporting-outcomes/SKILL.md) | Holds every reply to two lines and a question: the verdict, the next step, the offer |
| [remove-stale-files](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/remove-stale-files/SKILL.md) | Deletes what earlier versions of this plugin left behind, and the forks that shadow it |

## This repo is its own marketplace

![The repo hosts the plugin it develops; a directory source loads the working tree](docs/diagrams/png/03-its-own-marketplace.png)

The units are developed in the same tree that serves them, so they are used the way they
ship. If you are working on the plugin, add this directory as the marketplace source and
restart the session to load an edit — including one you have not committed yet.

`.sessions/` holds the raw agent transcripts, copied byte for byte out of
`~/.claude/projects/`, unfiltered. A log informs; it never binds. The code binds on what is
true now, the issue binds on what a change may touch, and a log that seems to forbid
something is only a previous session's situation.

## Contributing

`reviewing-artifacts` gates a skill, `reviewing-phrasing` and `reviewing-typography` gate a
document, and both gates run on this repo's own files before they land. Diagrams are SVG
sources committed alongside PNGs rendered by an explicit command:

    rsvg-convert -z 2 docs/diagrams/<name>.svg -o docs/diagrams/png/<name>.png

## License

MIT, as declared in
[plugin.json](plugins/agent-workflows/.claude-plugin/plugin.json).

content.text:
**REVISE** — three accuracy claims overreach, chiefly *"Fourteen skills, each stopping for a person"* in the opening line, which is not true of the four review gates or of `reporting-outcomes`.

Next: fix the three claims, then settle the two terminology slips.

Run it, or see the findings?

| # | Sev | Location | What's wrong | Smallest fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | high | line 5, opening | *"Fourteen skills, each stopping for a person."* Six do; `reporting-outcomes` shapes a reply and never gates, and the four review skills return a verdict. The false half sits in the sentence a newcomer reads first | *"Six of them are the spine, each stopping for a person; the rest gate what the spine produces."* |
| 2 | med | line 13, Requirements | *"`rsvg-convert` — only for `gen-readme`"* is listed as a requirement, but `gen-readme` states *"If rsvg-convert is absent, use the project's own renderer and record THAT command."* A reader without it will think they cannot install | move it out of Requirements, into the Contributing block where the render command already lives |
| 3 | med | line 95, Contributing | *"both gates run on this repo's own files before they land"* — nothing enforces that. No CI, no hook; it is a practice, and stated as a mechanism | *"…are run on this repo's own files before they land"*, or name it as the convention it is |
| 4 | med | lines 25 and 85 | `unit` and `skill` both name the same thing, five words apart in one case. One term per concept: the reader has to decide whether a unit is something else | `skill` throughout — it is the word the install command and the docs use |
| 5 | low | 6 em dashes, 8 per 1,000 words | From the script. Three are earned: the parenthetical list on line 39 has internal commas, and lines 33 and 87 turn sharply. Three are punctuation by habit — lines 13, 52, 75 | comma on 13, full stop on 52, colon in the table cell on 75 |
| 6 | low | License | *"MIT, as declared in `plugin.json`"* is true and there is no `LICENSE` file, so the claim resolves to a JSON key rather than a license text | add `LICENSE`, or say the file is not there yet |

**Script hits, ruled.** The 3 "exclamations" are `![…]` image syntax — false positives. The em-dash rate is the one real hit, and only half of it stands.

**What the script cannot reach, judged by reading:** no restatement found, no rule-of-three, no unearned hedge; sentence lengths vary; the first sentence of each section states its point. The structure matches current convention — a runnable command sits within the first screen, and the deep material is linked rather than inlined.

1	# agent-workflows
2	
3	A Claude Code plugin that carries one piece of work from a remark in a session to merged:
4	file the issue, claim it, do the work, judge what state it actually reached, open the
5	change request, land it. Six skills make that spine, each stopping for a person. Eight more
6	plan it, gate what it produces, and clean up after it. Nothing auto-runs the next.
7	
8	## Requirements
9	
10	- [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs) with plugin support
11	- `gh` or `glab`, installed and authenticated. Every step that touches an issue or a change
12	  request goes through one of them, and the skills derive which from `git remote`
13	
14	## Install
15	
16	    /plugin marketplace add dogkeeper886/agent-workflows
17	    /plugin install agent-workflows@agent-workflows
18	
19	Then ask for what you want in your own words, or invoke a skill by name:
20	
21	    /agent-workflows:file-issue the parser drops trailing commas
22	    /agent-workflows:take-issue 42
23	
24	The namespaced form always reaches the installed skill. A bare `/file-issue` reaches a local
25	copy of that name when your project has one.
26	
27	## How it works
28	
29	![The spine: six skills from a remark to merged](docs/diagrams/png/01-the-spine.png)
30	
31	The issue is the portal. When you say *"merge it"* you say nothing about the issue, the
32	branch, or what was discussed three days ago — `land-pr` walks back from the change request
33	to the issue to the branch. Without that join every step would need you to carry context
34	forward, which is the drift this exists to remove.
35	
36	**`review-work` is the reason the chain is worth having.** A step that always advanced
37	would be a formality. Four of its five outcomes send the work somewhere other than a change
38	request, and those four — half done, stuck, two tasks under one number, never started — are
39	the states that otherwise go unrecorded.
40	
41	**The toolkit keeps no state of its own.** No story file, no plan file, no index. The
42	issue, its labels, the branch and the change request live on the platform, which is the one
43	place both a person and an agent can read.
44	
45	## Not all work ends in a diff
46	
47	![The fork after do-task: a diff goes to a change request, evidence closes the issue](docs/diagrams/png/02-diff-or-evidence.png)
48	
49	A cert rotated, a cluster restarted, data migrated: the act is the deliverable. `do-task`
50	performs it, records the command, its output and the before-and-after state on the issue,
51	and closes it. No branch is cut, and no change request is ever opened. That is also why
52	`take-issue` cuts a branch only when a diff is coming.
53	
54	`file-issue` carries the same fork upstream, with a template per kind:
55	[bug](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/bug.md) ·
56	[task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/task.md) ·
57	[docs](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/docs.md) ·
58	[environment](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/environment.md) ·
59	[operation](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/operation.md).
60	
61	## The skills
62	
63	| Skill | What it does |
64	|---|---|
65	| [file-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md) | Turns something said in a session into an issue a cold agent can act on, and copies the session log beside it |
66	| [take-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/take-issue/SKILL.md) | Reads the issue whole, refuses it back when it cannot be started, or claims it and stops before any work |
67	| [do-task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/do-task/SKILL.md) | Writes and commits the change, or performs the act and captures the evidence |
68	| [review-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-work/SKILL.md) | Judges which of five states the work reached, and routes it there |
69	| [open-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/open-pr/SKILL.md) | Pushes the branch and opens the change request, linked so the issue closes on merge |
70	| [land-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/land-pr/SKILL.md) | Merges at a pinned SHA after a person answers whether they reviewed and tested it, then cleans up |
71	| [plan-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/plan-work/SKILL.md) | Splits work too large for one issue, grouped with whatever the platform already provides |
72	| [gen-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/gen-readme/SKILL.md) | Writes a README from the code, with one rendered diagram per key point |
73	| [review-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-readme/SKILL.md) | Gates a README on three counts: useful to a newcomer, true to the code, and readable |
74	| [reviewing-artifacts](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-artifacts/SKILL.md) | Gates the files an agent reads: skills, commands, rules. Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT |
75	| [reviewing-phrasing](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-phrasing/SKILL.md) | Reviews the words of a human-read document, greping the mechanical tells first |
76	| [reviewing-typography](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-typography/SKILL.md) | Reviews how such a document looks, the way a UI designer would |
77	| [reporting-outcomes](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reporting-outcomes/SKILL.md) | Holds every reply to two lines and a question: the verdict, the next step, the offer |
78	| [remove-stale-files](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/remove-stale-files/SKILL.md) | Deletes what earlier versions of this plugin left behind, and the forks that shadow it |
79	
80	## This repo is its own marketplace
81	
82	![The repo hosts the plugin it develops; a directory source loads the working tree](docs/diagrams/png/03-its-own-marketplace.png)
83	
84	The skills are developed in the same tree that serves them, so they are used the way they
85	ship. If you are working on the plugin, add this directory as the marketplace source and
86	restart the session to load an edit — including one you have not committed yet.
87	
88	`.sessions/` holds the raw agent transcripts, copied byte for byte out of
89	`~/.claude/projects/`, unfiltered. A log informs; it never binds. The code binds on what is
90	true now, the issue binds on what a change may touch, and a log that seems to forbid
91	something is only a previous session's situation.
92	
93	## Contributing
94	
95	`reviewing-artifacts` gates a skill, `reviewing-phrasing` and `reviewing-typography` gate a
96	document. By convention both are run on this repo's own files before they land; nothing
97	enforces it. Diagrams are SVG sources committed alongside PNGs rendered by an explicit
98	command, `rsvg-convert` by default:
99	
100	    rsvg-convert -z 2 docs/diagrams/<name>.svg -o docs/diagrams/png/<name>.png
101	
102	## License
103	
104	MIT, as declared in
105	[plugin.json](plugins/agent-workflows/.claude-plugin/plugin.json).

1	---
2	name: reviewing-typography
3	description: |
4	  Reviews how a human-read document looks — a README, prose and tables in docs/, an HTML
5	  page — and returns PASS or REVISE. Works the way a UI designer does: group the content,
6	  space the groups so the inner gap is smaller than the outer one, emphasize by dimming
7	  what is not the point rather than shouting what is, hold the level count low, and judge
8	  the page whole rather than section by section. Judges the look; the words are a separate
9	  review.
10	when_to_use: |
11	  Use whenever a document a person will read is written or restructured — a README, a
12	  guide, release notes, an HTML page — and before it reaches its reader. Also on request:
13	  "does this read okay", "make this scannable", "why does this look like a wall", "clean
14	  up the formatting", "too many headings". Reach for it on a doc that is factually right
15	  and still hard to get through, which is the case nobody thinks to ask about.
16	argument-hint: "[doc-path]"
17	---
18	
19	# Reviewing typography
20	
21	Target: $ARGUMENTS — a document path, or the one just written or edited.
22	
23	**A document a person reads is a UI.** Strip its formatting and it is a bunch of text with
24	no point of focus. The levers differ from a screen — no fonts to set in markdown — but the
25	job is identical: let the eye find the point without reading everything first.
26	
27	Markdown gives you four levers: **heading level** is size and weight, **blank lines** are
28	spacing, **bold and italic** are weight, and **paragraph and list length** decide whether
29	the page reads as structure or as soup. HTML adds colour, contrast and elevation.
30	
31	A marker is a symptom, not a verdict. Something is a finding when it costs the reader,
32	never because it matched a pattern. A clean document is reported clean.
33	
34	## The method
35	
36	Run it in this order. Each step invalidates the ones after it, so fixing out of order
37	means doing the later work twice.
38	
39	    1. GROUP      what belongs together, before touching any formatting
40	    2. SPACE      inner gap smaller than outer gap — always
41	    3. EMPHASIZE  by dimming the rest, not by shouting the point
42	    4. LEVEL      as few heading depths as the content truly has
43	    5. ZOOM OUT   judge the whole page, not the section you are in
44	
45	### 1. Group
46	
47	Read the content and mark what is one thing. A title and its subtitle are one group. A
48	list and its lead-in are one group. Two sections that happen to be adjacent are not.
49	
50	Do this before looking at a single `#` or `**`. Formatting applied before grouping is
51	decoration, and decoration is what the rest of this skill exists to remove.
52	
53	### 2. Space
54	
55	**The gap inside a group must be smaller than the gap around it.** This is the one rule
56	here that is close to absolute — break it and grouping collapses, no matter how correct
57	everything else is.
58	
59	    ✗ collapsed                      ✓ grouped
60	    ## Setup                         ## Setup
61	                                     Install it, then run it.
62	    Install it, then run it.
63	                                     - step one
64	    - step one                       - step two
65	                                     
66	    - step two                       ## Usage
67	    
68	    ## Usage
69	
70	On the left every gap is one blank line, so the heading, the prose, the two steps and the
71	next section all read as five peers. On the right the list is tight, the section break is
72	loose, and the shape is visible before a word is read.
73	
74	Markdown gives you three sizes of gap and no more: **none** (adjacent lines), **one blank
75	line**, and **a heading or `---`**. Spend them in that order — tightest inside, loosest
76	between.
77	
78	In HTML the same rule has real numbers behind it. Pick one spacing unit and step it —
79	half a unit inside a group, one to two units between — rather than choosing a fresh value
80	each time. Padding is the outer gap for anything boxed: a card's own padding must exceed
81	the gaps between the things inside it, or the box stops reading as a container.
82	
83	**Start loose and tighten.** Add the breaks generously, then remove the ones that separate
84	things which belong together. Extra whitespace costs a reader almost nothing; crowding
85	costs them the structure. Never start tight and add space where it seems needed — that
86	route ends at uniform spacing, which is the collapsed case above.
87	
88	**Consistency beats correctness.** A document that spaces every group the same wrong way
89	still reads: the reader learns the convention and applies it. A document that mixes three
90	conventions cannot be learned at all. So prefer one rule applied everywhere to a better
91	rule applied unevenly, and when you find inconsistency, say which convention should win.
92	
93	### 3. Emphasize
94	
95	**You cannot raise the important line. You can only lower the rest.**
96	
97	When every paragraph opens `**Label:**`, the bold is not emphasis, it is the body text.
98	The fix is never more bold on the thing that matters — it is removing bold from the twenty
99	things that do not.
100	
101	Weight, size and position are the three levers, and they compound: a short line, set as a
102	heading, at the top of its group, needs no bold at all. Reach for bold last, on the few
103	things a reader should land on.
104	
105	In HTML the same rule runs through contrast: the important text sits at high contrast and
106	everything else is dimmed toward the background. Headings do not go to maximum brightness —
107	that is harsh to read; the separation comes from lowering the surrounding text instead.
108	
109	### 4. Level
110	
111	**Almost no document needs a third heading depth.** A page of `##` with `###` where it
112	genuinely nests is the normal case. A nested heading over every two sentences is sprawl,
113	and it flattens the hierarchy it appears to create — five levels read the same as one.
114	
115	Markdown fuses two things a UI keeps apart: the heading level is both the document
116	structure and the visual weight. You cannot mark something structurally minor and visually
117	prominent. So pick the level for how it should *look* to a reader scanning, and accept the
118	structure that follows — the reader sees the look, not the outline.
119	
120	HTML separates them, and that separation is the point: `<h1>`–`<h6>` carry the outline for
121	a screen reader and a search engine, and CSS carries the weight. Code the level for the
122	document's real structure, then style it for the visual one. A heading skipped or
123	mis-levelled to get a size is a finding even when it looks right, because the outline is
124	what assistive technology navigates by.
125	
126	### 5. Zoom out
127	
128	Weight and size are relative. A `##` reads large in a short document and small in a long
129	one; a bold run stands out on a plain page and vanishes on a busy one. So judge the whole
130	document, not the paragraph in front of you.
131	
132	**The strip test.** Remove every `#`, `**` and `-` in your head and read what is left. If
133	the document is still navigable, the formatting is doing its job — supporting a structure
134	the content already has. If it collapses into undifferentiated text, the formatting was
135	carrying structure the writing never had, and that is the finding: fix the writing, not
136	the markup.
137	
138	## Markers
139	
140	Fast checks. Each one is a candidate, not a verdict — the method above rules on it.
141	
142	| Marker | What it usually means | Target |
143	|---|---|---|
144	| Every paragraph opens `**Label:**` | Emphasis spent as body text | Dim the rest; bold the few real anchors |
145	| Uniform blank lines everywhere | step 2 skipped — groups collapsed | Tight inside, loose between |
146	| Four or more heading depths | Structure invented, not found | Two, occasionally three |
147	| Prose chopped into bullets | A list because lists look organized | Lists for peers; prose for an argument |
148	| Every section the same length | Symmetry serving the doc, not the reader | The length each point needs |
149	| A long paragraph with no break | No entry point for the eye | A break at the natural boundary |
150	| Emoji headings, a rule between every section, a one-row table | Decoration | The plain shape the content asks for |
151	
152	In HTML, four more:
153	
154	| Marker | What it usually means | Target |
155	|---|---|---|
156	| Heading levels skipped, or chosen for size | Outline sacrificed to appearance | Level for structure, CSS for weight |
157	| Body text at maximum contrast | Nothing left to dim for emphasis | Body slightly muted, so headings separate without shouting |
158	| Many one-off spacing values | No system — every gap guessed | One unit, stepped |
159	| A card whose padding is tighter than its contents' gaps | The container stops containing | Padding exceeds the inner gaps |
160	
161	## Steps
162	
163	Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
164	
165	    Task Progress:
166	    - [ ] Groups marked, before reading any formatting
167	    - [ ] Inner-vs-outer gap checked on every group
168	    - [ ] Emphasis counted — is bold the exception or the body?
169	    - [ ] Heading depths counted
170	    - [ ] Strip test run on the whole document
171	    - [ ] Verdict reported
172	
173	1. **Scope it.** Which document. If unclear, ask.
174	2. **Run the five steps in order**, whole document, top to bottom.
175	3. **Report** (below).
176	4. **Fix, if asked.** Smallest change that lands the look — a break at a boundary, weight
177	   taken off labels that were never anchors. Leave what already reads well.
178	
179	## Report
180	
181	Two lines and a question:
182	
183	    REVISE — every gap is one blank line, so the six groups read as one list.
184	    Next: tighten inside the groups and break between them.
185	    Run it, or see the findings?
186	
187	- **PASS** — the eye finds the point; grouping and emphasis hold.
188	- **REVISE** — findings, each naming the step it failed and the smallest fix.
189	
190	Findings, what was checked, and the trace are prepared and held until asked. Cite the step
191	each finding came from — a fix at step 2 changes what step 3 should be, so the order is
192	part of the finding.

    3. EMPHASIZE  by dimming the rest, not by shouting the point
    4. LEVEL      as few heading depths as the content truly has
    5. ZOOM OUT   judge the whole page, not the section you are in

### 1. Group

Read the content and mark what is one thing. A title and its subtitle are one group. A
list and its lead-in are one group. Two sections that happen to be adjacent are not.

Do this before looking at a single `#` or `**`. Formatting applied before grouping is
decoration, and decoration is what the rest of this skill exists to remove.

### 2. Space

**The gap inside a group must be smaller than the gap around it.** This is the one rule
here that is close to absolute — break it and grouping collapses, no matter how correct
everything else is.

    ✗ collapsed                      ✓ grouped
    ## Setup                         ## Setup
                                     Install it, then run it.
    Install it, then run it.
                                     - step one
    - step one                       - step two
                                     
    - step two                       ## Usage
    
    ## Usage

On the left every gap is one blank line, so the heading, the prose, the two steps and the
next section all read as five peers. On the right the list is tight, the section break is
loose, and the shape is visible before a word is read.

Markdown gives you three sizes of gap and no more: **none** (adjacent lines), **one blank
line**, and **a heading or `---`**. Spend them in that order — tightest inside, loosest
between.

In HTML the same rule has real numbers behind it. Pick one spacing unit and step it —
half a unit inside a group, one to two units between — rather than choosing a fresh value
each time. Padding is the outer gap for anything boxed: a card's own padding must exceed
the gaps between the things inside it, or the box stops reading as a container.

**Start loose and tighten.** Add the breaks generously, then remove the ones that separate
things which belong together. Extra whitespace costs a reader almost nothing; crowding
costs them the structure. Never start tight and add space where it seems needed — that
route ends at uniform spacing, which is the collapsed case above.

**Consistency beats correctness.** A document that spaces every group the same wrong way
still reads: the reader learns the convention and applies it. A document that mixes three
conventions cannot be learned at all. So prefer one rule applied everywhere to a better
rule applied unevenly, and when you find inconsistency, say which convention should win.

### 3. Emphasize

**You cannot raise the important line. You can only lower the rest.**

When every paragraph opens `**Label:**`, the bold is not emphasis, it is the body text.
The fix is never more bold on the thing that matters — it is removing bold from the twenty
things that do not.

Weight, size and position are the three levers, and they compound: a short line, set as a
heading, at the top of its group, needs no bold at all. Reach for bold last, on the few
things a reader should land on.

In HTML the same rule runs through contrast: the important text sits at high contrast and
everything else is dimmed toward the background. Headings do not go to maximum brightness —
that is harsh to read; the separation comes from lowering the surrounding text instead.

### 4. Level

**Almost no document needs a third heading depth.** A page of `##` with `###` where it
genuinely nests is the normal case. A nested heading over every two sentences is sprawl,
and it flattens the hierarchy it appears to create — five levels read the same as one.

Markdown fuses two things a UI keeps apart: the heading level is both the document
structure and the visual weight. You cannot mark something structurally minor and visually
prominent. So pick the level for how it should *look* to a reader scanning, and accept the
structure that follows — the reader sees the look, not the outline.

HTML separates them, and that separation is the point: `<h1>`–`<h6>` carry the outline for
a screen reader and a search engine, and CSS carries the weight. Code the level for the
document's real structure, then style it for the visual one. A heading skipped or
mis-levelled to get a size is a finding even when it looks right, because the outline is
what assistive technology navigates by.

### 5. Zoom out

Weight and size are relative. A `##` reads large in a short document and small in a long
one; a bold run stands out on a plain page and vanishes on a busy one. So judge the whole
document, not the paragraph in front of you.

**The strip test.** Remove every `#`, `**` and `-` in your head and read what is left. If
the document is still navigable, the formatting is doing its job — supporting a structure
the content already has. If it collapses into undifferentiated text, the formatting was
carrying structure the writing never had, and that is the finding: fix the writing, not
the markup.

## Markers

Fast checks. Each one is a candidate, not a verdict — the method above rules on it.

| Marker | What it usually means | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Every paragraph opens `**Label:**` | Emphasis spent as body text | Dim the rest; bold the few real anchors |
| Uniform blank lines everywhere | step 2 skipped — groups collapsed | Tight inside, loose between |
| Four or more heading depths | Structure invented, not found | Two, occasionally three |
| Prose chopped into bullets | A list because lists look organized | Lists for peers; prose for an argument |
| Every section the same length | Symmetry serving the doc, not the reader | The length each point needs |
| A long paragraph with no break | No entry point for the eye | A break at the natural boundary |
| Emoji headings, a rule between every section, a one-row table | Decoration | The plain shape the content asks for |

In HTML, four more:

| Marker | What it usually means | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Heading levels skipped, or chosen for size | Outline sacrificed to appearance | Level for structure, CSS for weight |
| Body text at maximum contrast | Nothing left to dim for emphasis | Body slightly muted, so headings separate without shouting |
| Many one-off spacing values | No system — every gap guessed | One unit, stepped |
| A card whose padding is tighter than its contents' gaps | The container stops containing | Padding exceeds the inner gaps |

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Groups marked, before reading any formatting
    - [ ] Inner-vs-outer gap checked on every group
    - [ ] Emphasis counted — is bold the exception or the body?
    - [ ] Heading depths counted
    - [ ] Strip test run on the whole document
    - [ ] Verdict reported

1. **Scope it.** Which document. If unclear, ask.
2. **Run the five steps in order**, whole document, top to bottom.
3. **Report** (below).
4. **Fix, if asked.** Smallest change that lands the look — a break at a boundary, weight
   taken off labels that were never anchors. Leave what already reads well.

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    REVISE — every gap is one blank line, so the six groups read as one list.
    Next: tighten inside the groups and break between them.
    Run it, or see the findings?

- **PASS** — the eye finds the point; grouping and emphasis hold.
- **REVISE** — findings, each naming the step it failed and the smallest fix.

Findings, what was checked, and the trace are prepared and held until asked. Cite the step
each finding came from — a fix at step 2 changes what step 3 should be, so the order is
part of the finding.

1	---
2	name: file-issue
3	description: |
4	  Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
5	  copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
6	  reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
7	  searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the
8	  words it was made in rather than paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone
9	  else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to.
10	when_to_use: |
11	  Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
12	  "this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
13	  Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
14	  "this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
15	  upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
16	  expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
17	  "that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
18	  problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
19	  surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
20	  goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
21	  for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.
22	argument-hint: "[what to file]"
23	---
24	
25	# File an issue
26	
27	Target: $ARGUMENTS — what to file, or the thing just discussed.
28	
29	**The issue is a portal, not a record.** Everything after it resolves backwards through
30	it: a branch takes its name, a commit cites it, a PR closes it, and an agent picking up
31	cold reads it first. What it cannot do is carry the reasoning that produced it — an issue
32	body is a summary by nature, and summarising is where the intent shifts.
33	
34	So the split is: **the issue states the decision and the test; the session log holds the
35	reasoning.** The issue links to the log rather than absorbing it.
36	
37	**The point is to make the platform pay off.** Every act below is a `gh` or `glab` call a
38	person could make themselves. The value is not having to remember which, not having to
39	notice the two CLIs disagree, and not having to write a body that a stranger can act on
40	from a standing start. Where this skill would add a step the platform does not need, it is
41	wrong — process invented on top of a tracker is a cost the tracker was supposed to remove.
42	
43	## 0. Which platform
44	
45	**Derive it, never assume it.** `git remote get-url origin` names the host. No address
46	belongs in this file: one a person has to keep correct goes stale silently.
47	
48	| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |

## What

> "let's do do-task > reviewing-finish (we need it to identify half done, need revise (stock or can solve), done, not start yet (or block), ...etc or route to plan if multiple task, fix required) > open-pr > land-pr"

> "the goal of setup-agent-workflows changed now… for the story files, rule files in repo. i recommend remove… i prefer same idea of detect then delete. doc file always stale while time past. become pain of error or mislead for future agent cause expensive. after rca you only get regret."

Rebuild the plugin as one workflow that carries a single piece of work from a remark in a
session to merged, mapped onto GitHub Flow one unit at a time, and delete everything the
old shape left behind.

## Why

The old set picked a change up at a commit and handed it to a ship tail. It assumed the
work was already understood, already correct, and already a diff. Three things broke on
that assumption:

- Nothing recorded the states a piece of work actually reaches. A step that always advances
  is a formality, and half-finished or stuck work left no trace.
- Work that ends in an act rather than a patch — a cert rotated, a migration run — had no
  path at all. It was made to look like a diff or it went untracked.
- Values were resolved through `.claude/rules/project-profile.md`, so a unit stopped when a
  project had not written one, and the file went stale the moment either side moved.

## Plan

1. `file-issue` — create the portal every later step resolves back to, with a template per
   kind → verify: an issue filed from a cold start needs no question to act on
2. `take-issue` — read the issue whole, refuse it back when it cannot be started, claim it
   and stop → verify: a branch is cut only where a diff is coming
3. `do-task` — commit the change, or perform the act and capture the evidence → verify:
   an evidence issue closes with its command, output and before-and-after state
4. `review-work` — judge which of five states the work reached and route it there →
   verify: only one of the five reaches a change request
5. `open-pr`, `land-pr` — push and link, then merge at a pinned SHA behind a person's
   answer → verify: the issue closes on merge by keyword, not by hand
6. Delete the values layer and the documents that described the old shape; replace the
   adoption unit with one that detects and deletes them → verify:
   `scripts/check-refs.sh plugins` reports no reference to anything retired
7. Write the README from the code → verify: every claim and link resolves against the tree

## Expected outcome

A person says what they want in their own words and the right unit fires; each unit stops
for a human decision; the issue and the platform hold all the state; and a document that
has gone stale is deleted rather than maintained.

## Done when

- [x] Six units exist and run in order: `file-issue`, `take-issue`, `do-task`,
      `review-work`, `open-pr`, `land-pr`
- [x] `review-work` returns five states and four of them do not advance
- [x] Work that ends in evidence closes on its issue and never opens a change request
- [x] No unit resolves a value from `.claude/rules/project-profile.md`
- [x] No file in `plugins/` cites a skill or rule that does not exist, except the remove
      lists, which name retired things by design
- [x] `README.md` exists, with a rendered diagram per key point and every link resolving

## What's next

The two open questions this leaves are whether accumulated session logs stay workable as
they grow, and whether `remove-stale-files` should also run against a project that has
never adopted the plugin.

## Context

Session: `.sessions/f4492b01-e778-4d0a-938d-4455205b3635.jsonl` — the redesign itself,
from the first flow chart to `land-pr`.
Session: `.sessions/da3e9fe4-bc6c-4bb7-b2c9-21cdca589cf1.jsonl` — the adoption unit
becoming `remove-stale-files`, the plugin descriptions, and the README.

Read as background, never as specification. The code binds on what is true now, this issue
binds on what the change may touch, and the log only informs.

## Out of scope

- The build half — spec, tickets, implement. Another toolkit's job.
- A planning layer of this plugin's own. `plan-work` groups with whatever the platform
  already provides and invents nothing.
- Editing `agent-workflows-runner`. Its `qa-*` commands still resolve their own sections
  from `project-profile.md`, and that file survives for them.
- A `LICENSE` file. `plugin.json` declares MIT; the file itself is a separate decision.

1	---
2	name: review-work
3	description: |
4	  Judges what state finished work is actually in, and routes it there. Checks the
5	  acceptance line against the work rather than against the claim about it, sweeps what the
6	  change left behind, and sends the result onward, back for more, back to the issue, or up
7	  for splitting. Only one of its five outcomes reaches a change request, which is the point
8	  of having it.
9	when_to_use: |
10	  Use after work has been done and before anything ships it, every time, whatever kind it
11	  is. Triggers: "review this", "check my work", "is this done", "did that work", "have a
12	  look", "ready to ship?", and the end of any do-task run. Reach for it on evidence work
13	  too, where there is no diff to read and the question is whether the act is proven. Not
14	  for judging prose or a document's look, and not for opening a change request.
15	argument-hint: "[issue-number]"
16	---
17	
18	# Review the work
19	
20	Target: $ARGUMENTS — the issue whose work is being judged.
21	
22	**The author already said what state it is in. This decides whether that is true.** An
23	author grading their own work grades it done, not from dishonesty but because the gap
24	between what was intended and what exists is invisible from inside. That gap is the only
25	thing this unit looks for.
26	
27	**Four of its five outcomes do not advance.** A reviewer that always passes work along is a
28	formality, and the four other states are the ones that go unrecorded today: work quietly
29	half-finished, work stuck with nobody told, two tasks wearing one number, work never
30	started because a precondition was false.
31	
32	## 0. Which platform
33	
34	Derive it from `git remote get-url origin`. Only the verbs this unit needs:
35	
36	| | GitHub — `gh` | GitLab — `glab` |
37	|---|---|---|
38	| comment | `gh issue comment <N> --body "…"` | `glab issue note <N> -m "…"` |
39	| unassign | `gh issue edit <N> --remove-assignee @me` | `glab issue update <N> --unassign` |
40	| move state | `gh issue edit <N> --add-label <a> --remove-label <b>` | `glab issue update <N> --label <a> --unlabel <b>` |
41	
42	## 1. Read both sides
43	
44	**What was asked**: the issue, its acceptance line, its `Out of scope`, and any comments
45	added since it was claimed.
46	
47	**What exists**: the diff against the branch point, or for evidence work, the commands and
48	output recorded on the issue.
49	
50	Read them in that order. Reading the work first anchors you to what was built, and the
51	question is whether what was built is what was asked for.
52	
53	## 2. Does the acceptance line hold
54	
55	Take each box in `Done when` and answer it from the work, not from the report about the
56	work. A claim is satisfied when it was observed.
57	
58	**Run what the project runs.** Not because the author would not have, but because "the
59	suite passed" and "the suite passed on what is committed" are different sentences, and only
60	one of them is checkable now.
61	
62	Find it in what the repo actually declares: a package manifest's scripts, a `Makefile`, a CI
63	workflow, a task runner's config, the commands the project's own instructions name. Run the
64	full set here rather than the one file that was being iterated on.
65	
66	**Where nothing runnable exists** — a docs repo, a markdown toolkit — say so plainly and
67	move on. That is a fact about how far this verdict can reach, not a failure, and "there is
68	no test suite" tells a reader more than an unqualified *verified*.
69	
70	**For evidence work, the question is different**: does the record prove the act happened?
71	Commands as run, output verbatim, before and after state. A tidy summary of an operation is
72	not evidence of it, and neither is the absence of an error.
73	
74	**Scope, both directions.** Work that widened past `Out of scope` is a finding even when
75	every added line is good. Work that quietly narrowed is the more common one, and it looks
76	like done.
77	
78	## 3. What did it leave behind
79	
80	The part no diff reader does, because the evidence is repo-wide rather than in the diff:
81	
82	- **Debris this change added.** Debug output, commented-out blocks, a skipped test, a
83	  hardcoded stub, a flag flipped and forgotten. Only what this change added; pre-existing
84	  mess gets mentioned, not swept.
85	- **Orphans this change made.** An import, a file, a fixture whose last user went with the
86	  change. Verify by search before removing anything, and removing a whole file needs
87	  approval rather than judgement.
88	- **Facts this change updated in one place and not another.** A count in prose, a version in
89	  a diagram, a name in a generated artifact. These are the ones that survive every review,
90	  because each copy reads correctly on its own.
91	
92	**Report what you find; do not quietly fix it.** A reviewer that edits on its own initiative
93	hands back work nobody has seen, and the author cannot tell a finding from a change. Fix on
94	request, smallest blast radius first, and re-run the tooling afterwards — a cleanup that
95	breaks the build is worse than the debris it removed. **Removing a whole file needs explicit
96	approval**, whatever the search says.
97	
98	## 4. Route it
99	
100	Five states, and the destination is part of the judgment:
101	
102	| State | Where it goes | What has to be true |
103	|---|---|---|
104	| **done** | onward — a change request, or the evidence close | Every acceptance box observed, scope held, nothing left behind |
105	| **half done** | back for more work | Real progress, and the remainder is clear enough to name |
106	| **stuck** | back to the issue, unassigned | Blocked on something the doer cannot resolve |
107	| **more than one task** | up, for splitting | Two or more deliverables wearing one number |
108	| **not started** | back to the issue | A precondition was false before anything was touched |
109	
110	**Disagreeing with the author is the job.** If the work reports done and an acceptance box
111	is not observable, the state is half done and saying so is the entire value of this pass.
112	Agreement reached by not looking is worth nothing.
113	
114	**"Done" is the expensive one.** Everything downstream trusts it; the other four cost a
115	message.
116	
117	## 5. Record the route
118	
119	The judgment belongs on the issue, not only in the reply. Someone picking this up next week
120	reads the issue.
121	
122	- **done** — say so and what was checked. Nothing else moves; the change request or the
123	  evidence close handles the rest.
124	- **half done** — comment with what remains. Leave it assigned; it is still being worked.
125	- **stuck** — comment with what blocked it and who could unblock it, then unassign and move
126	  the state label back. An issue left assigned to someone who has stopped is invisible.
127	- **more than one task** — comment with where the seam is, so the split does not start from
128	  scratch.
129	- **not started** — comment with which precondition was false. That is usually a finding
130	  about the issue rather than the work.
131	
132	## Steps
133	
134	Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:
135	
136	    Task Progress:
137	    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
138	    - [ ] Read what was asked, then what exists, in that order
139	    - [ ] Every acceptance box answered from the work, not the report
140	    - [ ] Project tooling run, or its absence stated plainly
141	    - [ ] Scope checked both ways — widened and narrowed
142	    - [ ] Debris, orphans and half-updated facts found and reported
143	    - [ ] State decided, and disagreement with the author stated if any
144	    - [ ] Route recorded on the issue
145	
146	## Report
147	
148	Two lines and a question:
149	
150	    HALF DONE — reported done, but the second acceptance box has no test covering it.
151	    Next: add the test, then this passes.
152	    Run it, or see the findings?
153	
154	Passing reads the same, and says what made it a pass:
155	
156	    DONE — both acceptance boxes observed, suite green on the committed tree, nothing left
157	    behind.
158	    Next: open the change request.
159	
160	A route away from the work is still a verdict:
161	
162	    STUCK — the migration needs a maintenance window nobody has scheduled.
163	    Next: #52 unassigned and commented; someone books the window.
164	
165	The two that are easiest to leave unsaid, because neither feels like a result:
166	
167	    MORE THAN ONE TASK — the schema change is done; the UI half has not started and
168	    ships separately.
169	    Next: split #47, then this half is ready.
170	
171	    NOT STARTED — the precondition is false: staging is already on 16.
172	    Next: someone confirms whether #52 is stale before anything runs.
173	
174	The findings, the tooling output, the sweep and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

Take each box in `Done when` and answer it from the work, not from the report about the
work. A claim is satisfied when it was observed.

**Run what the project runs.** Not because the author would not have, but because "the
suite passed" and "the suite passed on what is committed" are different sentences, and only
one of them is checkable now.

Find it in what the repo actually declares: a package manifest's scripts, a `Makefile`, a CI
workflow, a task runner's config, the commands the project's own instructions name. Run the
full set here rather than the one file that was being iterated on.

**Where nothing runnable exists** — a docs repo, a markdown toolkit — say so plainly and
move on. That is a fact about how far this verdict can reach, not a failure, and "there is
no test suite" tells a reader more than an unqualified *verified*.

**For evidence work, the question is different**: does the record prove the act happened?
Commands as run, output verbatim, before and after state. A tidy summary of an operation is
not evidence of it, and neither is the absence of an error.

**Scope, both directions.** Work that widened past `Out of scope` is a finding even when
every added line is good. Work that quietly narrowed is the more common one, and it looks
like done.

## 3. What did it leave behind

The part no diff reader does, because the evidence is repo-wide rather than in the diff:

- **Debris this change added.** Debug output, commented-out blocks, a skipped test, a
  hardcoded stub, a flag flipped and forgotten. Only what this change added; pre-existing
  mess gets mentioned, not swept.
- **Orphans this change made.** An import, a file, a fixture whose last user went with the
  change. Verify by search before removing anything, and removing a whole file needs
  approval rather than judgement.
- **Facts this change updated in one place and not another.** A count in prose, a version in
  a diagram, a name in a generated artifact. These are the ones that survive every review,
  because each copy reads correctly on its own.

**Report what you find; do not quietly fix it.** A reviewer that edits on its own initiative
hands back work nobody has seen, and the author cannot tell a finding from a change. Fix on
request, smallest blast radius first, and re-run the tooling afterwards — a cleanup that
breaks the build is worse than the debris it removed. **Removing a whole file needs explicit
approval**, whatever the search says.

## 4. Route it

Five states, and the destination is part of the judgment:

| State | Where it goes | What has to be true |
|---|---|---|
| **done** | onward — a change request, or the evidence close | Every acceptance box observed, scope held, nothing left behind |
| **half done** | back for more work | Real progress, and the remainder is clear enough to name |
| **stuck** | back to the issue, unassigned | Blocked on something the doer cannot resolve |
| **more than one task** | up, for splitting | Two or more deliverables wearing one number |
| **not started** | back to the issue | A precondition was false before anything was touched |

**Disagreeing with the author is the job.** If the work reports done and an acceptance box
is not observable, the state is half done and saying so is the entire value of this pass.
Agreement reached by not looking is worth nothing.

**"Done" is the expensive one.** Everything downstream trusts it; the other four cost a
message.

## 5. Record the route

The judgment belongs on the issue, not only in the reply. Someone picking this up next week
reads the issue.

- **done** — say so and what was checked. Nothing else moves; the change request or the
  evidence close handles the rest.
- **half done** — comment with what remains. Leave it assigned; it is still being worked.
- **stuck** — comment with what blocked it and who could unblock it, then unassign and move
  the state label back. An issue left assigned to someone who has stopped is invisible.
- **more than one task** — comment with where the seam is, so the split does not start from
  scratch.
- **not started** — comment with which precondition was false. That is usually a finding
  about the issue rather than the work.

## Steps

Copy this checklist and tick each item as you finish it:

    Task Progress:
    - [ ] Platform derived from the git remote, not assumed
    - [ ] Read what was asked, then what exists, in that order
    - [ ] Every acceptance box answered from the work, not the report
    - [ ] Project tooling run, or its absence stated plainly
    - [ ] Scope checked both ways — widened and narrowed
    - [ ] Debris, orphans and half-updated facts found and reported
    - [ ] State decided, and disagreement with the author stated if any
    - [ ] Route recorded on the issue

## Report

Two lines and a question:

    HALF DONE — reported done, but the second acceptance box has no test covering it.
    Next: add the test, then this passes.
    Run it, or see the findings?

Passing reads the same, and says what made it a pass:

    DONE — both acceptance boxes observed, suite green on the committed tree, nothing left
    behind.
    Next: open the change request.

A route away from the work is still a verdict:

    STUCK — the migration needs a maintenance window nobody has scheduled.
    Next: #52 unassigned and commented; someone books the window.

The two that are easiest to leave unsaid, because neither feels like a result:

    MORE THAN ONE TASK — the schema change is done; the UI half has not started and
    ships separately.
    Next: split #47, then this half is ready.

    NOT STARTED — the precondition is false: staging is already on 16.
    Next: someone confirms whether #52 is stale before anything runs.

The findings, the tooling output, the sweep and the trace are prepared and held until asked.

Closes #175.

Rebuilds the plugin as one workflow that carries a piece of work from a remark in a session
to merged, and deletes what the old shape left behind. 29 commits.

## What changed

**The spine, six units, each stopping for a person.** `file-issue` creates the portal every
later step resolves back to, with a template per kind. `take-issue` reads the issue whole
and refuses it back when it cannot be started. `do-task` commits a diff, or performs an act
and records the evidence. `review-work` judges which of five states the work reached, and
four of the five do not advance. `open-pr` links so the issue closes on merge; `land-pr`
merges at a pinned SHA behind a person's answer.

declaration wins, and the platform is derived from `git remote` at run time.

nothing reads any more. What survived is the half that finds forked copies shadowing placed
units, and that half is deletion: it detects, shows, asks once, and removes. It never
writes.

the PNGs they render to.

`templates/CLAUDE.md` that was byte-identical to the repo's own.

  shadows. Deleting the wrong file in someone's project is the expensive failure here.

  stays workable.

1	# agent-workflows
2	
3	A Claude Code plugin that carries one piece of work from a remark in a session to merged:
4	file the issue, claim it, do the work, judge what state it actually reached, open the
5	change request, land it. Six skills make that spine, each stopping for a person. Eight more
6	plan it, gate what it produces, and clean up after it. Nothing auto-runs the next.
7	
8	## Requirements
9	
10	- [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs) with plugin support
11	- `gh` or `glab`, installed and authenticated. Every step that touches an issue or a change
12	  request goes through one of them, and the skills derive which from `git remote`
13	
14	## Install
15	
16	    /plugin marketplace add dogkeeper886/agent-workflows
17	    /plugin install agent-workflows@agent-workflows
18	
19	## Using it
20	
21	Ask for what you want in your own words, or invoke a skill by name:
22	
23	    /agent-workflows:file-issue the parser drops trailing commas
24	    /agent-workflows:take-issue 42
25	
26	The namespaced form always reaches the installed skill. A bare `/file-issue` reaches a local
27	copy of that name when your project has one.
28	
29	## How it works
30	
31	![The spine: six skills from a remark to merged](docs/diagrams/png/01-the-spine.png)
32	
33	The issue is the portal. When you say *"merge it"* you say nothing about the issue, the
34	branch, or what was discussed three days ago — `land-pr` walks back from the change request
35	to the issue to the branch. Without that join every step would need you to carry context
36	forward, which is the drift this exists to remove.
37	
38	**`review-work` is the reason the chain is worth having.** A step that always advanced
39	would be a formality. Four of its five outcomes send the work somewhere other than a change
40	request, and those four — half done, stuck, two tasks under one number, never started — are
41	the states that otherwise go unrecorded.
42	
43	**The toolkit keeps no state of its own.** No story file, no plan file, no index. The
44	issue, its labels, the branch and the change request live on the platform, which is the one
45	place both a person and an agent can read.
46	
47	## Not all work ends in a diff
48	
49	![The fork after do-task: a diff goes to a change request, evidence closes the issue](docs/diagrams/png/02-diff-or-evidence.png)
50	
51	A cert rotated, a cluster restarted, data migrated: the act is the deliverable. `do-task`
52	performs it, records the command, its output and the before-and-after state on the issue,
53	and closes it. No branch is cut, and no change request is ever opened. That is also why
54	`take-issue` cuts a branch only when a diff is coming.
55	
56	`file-issue` carries the same fork upstream, with a template per kind:
57	[bug](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/bug.md) ·
58	[task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/task.md) ·
59	[docs](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/docs.md) ·
60	[environment](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/environment.md) ·
61	[operation](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/templates/operation.md).
62	
63	## The skills
64	
65	### The spine
66	
67	| Skill | What it does |
68	|---|---|
69	| [file-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/file-issue/SKILL.md) | Turns something said in a session into an issue a cold agent can act on, and copies the session log beside it |
70	| [take-issue](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/take-issue/SKILL.md) | Reads the issue whole, refuses it back when it cannot be started, or claims it and stops before any work |
71	| [do-task](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/do-task/SKILL.md) | Writes and commits the change, or performs the act and captures the evidence |
72	| [review-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-work/SKILL.md) | Judges which of five states the work reached, and routes it there |
73	| [open-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/open-pr/SKILL.md) | Pushes the branch and opens the change request, linked so the issue closes on merge |
74	| [land-pr](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/land-pr/SKILL.md) | Merges at a pinned SHA after a person answers whether they reviewed and tested it, then cleans up |
75	
76	### Around it
77	
78	| Skill | What it does |
79	|---|---|
80	| [plan-work](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/plan-work/SKILL.md) | Splits work too large for one issue, grouped with whatever the platform already provides |
81	| [gen-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/gen-readme/SKILL.md) | Writes a README from the code, with one rendered diagram per key point |
82	| [review-readme](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/review-readme/SKILL.md) | Gates a README on three counts: useful to a newcomer, true to the code, and readable |
83	| [reviewing-artifacts](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-artifacts/SKILL.md) | Gates the files an agent reads: skills, commands, rules. Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT |
84	| [reviewing-phrasing](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-phrasing/SKILL.md) | Reviews the words of a human-read document, greping the mechanical tells first |
85	| [reviewing-typography](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reviewing-typography/SKILL.md) | Reviews how such a document looks, the way a UI designer would |
86	| [reporting-outcomes](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/reporting-outcomes/SKILL.md) | Holds every reply to two lines and a question: the verdict, the next step, the offer |
87	| [remove-stale-files](plugins/agent-workflows/skills/remove-stale-files/SKILL.md) | Deletes what earlier versions of this plugin left behind, and the forks that shadow it |
88	
89	## This repo is its own marketplace
90	
91	![The repo hosts the plugin it develops; a directory source loads the working tree](docs/diagrams/png/03-its-own-marketplace.png)
92	
93	The skills are developed in the same tree that serves them, so they are used the way they
94	ship. If you are working on the plugin, add this directory as the marketplace source and
95	restart the session to load an edit — including one you have not committed yet.
96	
97	## Session logs
98	
99	`.sessions/` holds the raw agent transcripts, copied byte for byte out of
100	`~/.claude/projects/`, unfiltered. A log informs; it never binds. The code binds on what is
101	true now, the issue binds on what a change may touch, and a log that seems to forbid
102	something is only a previous session's situation.
103	
104	## Contributing
105	
106	`reviewing-artifacts` gates a skill, `reviewing-phrasing` and `reviewing-typography` gate a
107	document. By convention both are run on this repo's own files before they land; nothing
108	enforces it. Diagrams are SVG sources committed alongside PNGs rendered by an explicit
109	command, `rsvg-convert` by default:
110	
111	    rsvg-convert -z 2 docs/diagrams/<name>.svg -o docs/diagrams/png/<name>.png
112	
113	## License
114	
115	MIT, as declared in
116	[plugin.json](plugins/agent-workflows/.claude-plugin/plugin.json).

- codebase-memory: Use the codebase knowledge graph for structural code queries. Triggers on: explore the codebase, understand the architecture, what functions exist, show me the structure, who calls this function, what does X call, trace the call chain, find callers of, show dependencies, impact analysis, dead code, unused functions, high fan-out, refactor candidates, code quality audit, graph query syntax, Cypher query examples, edge types, how to use search_graph.
- karpathy-guidelines: Behavioral guidelines to reduce common LLM coding mistakes. Use when writing, reviewing, or refactoring code to avoid overcomplication, make surgical changes, surface assumptions, and define verifiable success criteria.
- writing-agent-skills: Author, review, and refactor Agent Skills — SKILL.md frontmatter, description wording for reliable triggering, progressive disclosure across bundled files, workflow checklists, validator feedback loops, and evaluation-driven iteration. Use whenever the user is writing a new skill, editing or splitting an existing SKILL.md, migrating slash commands or prompts into skills, packaging skills into a plugin, debugging a skill that fails to trigger or triggers too often, or asking how skills should be structured — including when they describe the work as "turn this into a skill" or "make this reusable" without saying the word skill.
- agent-workflows:do-task: Does the work a claimed issue describes — writes and commits the change, or performs the
act and captures the evidence that it happened. Holds the scope the issue set, records
why in the commit message rather than only what, and ends by stating what state the work
is actually in rather than declaring it done. The write half of an issue; something else
judges whether it finished. - Use once an issue is claimed and the work should start, whatever kind it is — "implement
it", "fix it", "make the change", "go ahead", "do it". Code: "write the parser fix".
Docs: "update that README". Environment: "run the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate
the cert now", "run the migration", "restart it". Reach for it after take-issue has
claimed something, and when the user says do it on work already understood. Not for
choosing what to work on, not for opening a change request, and not for deciding whether
the result is good enough — each of those is somebody else's job.

- agent-workflows:file-issue: Turns something said in a session into a tracked issue that a cold agent can act on, and
copies the session log beside it wherever one can be had — always attempted, never a
reason to withhold the issue. Decides first whether the thing needs tracking at all,
searches for an existing issue before creating a second one, quotes the request in the
words it was made in rather than paraphrasing it, and states an acceptance test someone
else can check. Creates the portal every later step resolves back to. - Use whenever work is identified but not started, of any kind — not only code. Code:
"this is broken", "raise a bug", "we should track this", "someone should fix that".
Docs: "the README is wrong", "nobody can find how to run this", "that page is stale",
"this needs writing up". Environment: "staging is on the old version", "we should
upgrade that", "this config drifted", "we need a bigger instance". Operations: "the cert
expires next week", "someone has to rotate that key", "we need to migrate the data",
"that job needs re-running". Also the generic ones: "file an issue", "that's a separate
problem", "let's do that later", "add it to the backlog". Reach for it when a session
surfaces a second problem while working on a first, which is the case that most often
goes unrecorded, and when the thing is an act to perform rather than code to write. Not
for a question, a thing already underway, or a fix smaller than the issue describing it.

- agent-workflows:gen-readme: Writes a project's README from the code: researches current README convention on the
web, studies the repo from its ground truth rather than its existing docs, finds the key
points a newcomer needs first, draws every one of them as an SVG rendered to PNG, and
writes the file. Produces the README only — it does not open a PR, and review-readme
gates what it wrote. - Use whenever a README is about to be created or edited — before writing one from
scratch, and before changing an existing one. Covers "write the README", "generate a
README for this project", "our README is stale, redo it", "update the README", "document
this repo for newcomers", "write a README for ../other-repo" — and applies even when the
request is to touch one section rather than the whole file.

- agent-workflows:land-pr: Merges an approved change request and cleans up after it: the code lands in the default
branch, the branch is gone, the issue closes, the labels clear. Asks a person outright
whether the change was reviewed and tested at this exact head, records that answer, and
pins the merge to that SHA so a head that moved cannot slip through. Refuses to merge
without the answer. - Use when an open change request should land — "merge it", "merge PR 30", "land it",
"ship it", "close out #27", "the PR is approved", "merge and clean up". Being told to run
this is a request to reach the human gate, never the answer to it. Not for opening a
change request, and not for work that ends in evidence rather than a diff.

- agent-workflows:open-pr: Pushes a committed branch and opens the change request that carries it to a human, linked
to its issue so the issue closes on merge rather than by hand. Moves the commits onto a
branch first when they landed on the default one, gets the closure keyword right, and
stops for review. It does not merge, and it does not judge whether the work is good;
something before it did that. - Use when reviewed work is ready for a human to look at — "open a PR", "raise the merge
request", "push this up", "ship it", "put it up for review", "my commits are on main, get
them onto a branch". Reach for it after the work has been judged done, and when someone
says ship it meaning make it reviewable. Not for work that ends in evidence rather than a
diff, which closes on its issue and never reaches a change request. Not for merging.

- agent-workflows:plan-work: Splits work too large for one issue into issues that can each be delivered on their own,
and groups them with whatever the project already uses to group things — a milestone, a
project board, an epic. Decides first whether splitting is warranted at all, since most
work is not, and never invents a grouping the platform already provides. - Use when one issue is holding more than one deliverable — "break this down", "what are
the tasks", "this is too big", "split it", "that's really three things", "plan this
out", "make tickets for this". Also when take-issue reports that an issue is more than
one task, which is the case that arrives without anyone asking for a plan. Not for
ordinary work that happens to have several steps, and not for filing a single issue.

- agent-workflows:remove-stale-files: Finds and removes what this plugin's earlier versions wrote into a project: forked
commands and skills that shadow the placed units, rules and story files nothing reads
any more, and the sections this plugin wrote into `project-profile.md`. Shows every file
before touching one, and deletes only on a yes. It never adds: every edit it makes is a
removal. - Use whenever one of the files below is read, edited, or about to be created. Its
presence is the trigger; nobody has to ask for a cleanup. In `.claude/commands/`:
`dw-story`, `dw-plan`, `dw-tasks`, `dw-implement`, `dw-create-pr`, `dw-merge`,
`dw-review-story`, `dw-review-tasks`, `dw-review-implement`, `dw-review-pr`,
`dw-test-design`, `qw-plan`, `qw-cases`, `qw-review-plan`, `qw-review-cases`,
`qw-drift`. In `.claude/skills/`: `auditing-artifacts`, `auditing-readme`,
`ship-create-pr`, `ship-merge`, `reviewing-finish`, `doc-gen-readme`,
`doc-review-readme`, and a local copy of any name this plugin ships. In
`.claude/rules/`: `agent-report.md`, `anti-slop.md`, `dev-workflow.md`,
`doc-workflow.md`, `qa-workflow.md`, `ship-tail.md`, `profile-doctrine.md`, and the
sections this plugin wrote into `project-profile.md`. Elsewhere: `docs/stories/`,
`docs/agents/domain.md`, `docs/agents/issue-tracker.md`, `docs/agents/triage-labels.md`,
`CONTEXT.md`, and a `## How to report` or `## Agent skills` section in `CLAUDE.md` or
`AGENTS.md`. Also on request: "clean up .claude", "why are there two ship-merge", "is
this rule still read", "we retired that workflow, what is left". …
- agent-workflows:reporting-outcomes: Reports work in two lines and a question — the verdict, the one next step, and whether
the reader wants it run or wants the detail. Findings, what was checked, risks and
decisions are prepared and held; the reader acts on the next step or asks. Only a
blocked or failed next step brings its blocker up with it. Replaces the reply that mixes
progress, findings, reasoning and status into a narrative the reader has to mine. - Use whenever writing back about work — what was done, what was found, whether it worked,
where things stand, what is left, what broke, what is blocked — and the answer runs
longer than a line. Covers the everyday reply, not only a formal gate: a status update,
a summary of a run, a review verdict, a handoff note, an answer to "how did it go" or
"where are we". Reach for it even when nobody said the word "report", even when the
reply feels short enough to wing, and even when the news is good. The buried verdict is
the failure this prevents, and it is invisible to the person writing it.

- agent-workflows:review-readme: Gates a README before a person reads it, on three counts: it delivers for a newcomer,
it is true to the code, and it reads and looks right. Derives the key points from the
code and checks the README leads with them and ships a diagram for each, verifies every
command, path, env var and link against the source, and re-renders each diagram to catch
one that has drifted from what it is drawn from. Gates what gen-readme wrote, and any
README edited by hand. - Use whenever a README has just been created or edited, by this toolkit or by hand —
including an edit made without gen-readme, and an edit to a single section rather than
the whole file. Also on request: "review the README", "check the README is accurate",
"does the README still match the code", "gate this README before I open a PR". A README
changed and not gated reaches its reader unverified, so treat any write to one as the
trigger rather than waiting to be asked.

- agent-workflows:review-work: Judges what state finished work is actually in, and routes it there. Checks the
acceptance line against the work rather than against the claim about it, sweeps what the
change left behind, and sends the result onward, back for more, back to the issue, or up
for splitting. Only one of its five outcomes reaches a change request, which is the point
of having it. - Use after work has been done and before anything ships it, every time, whatever kind it
is. Triggers: "review this", "check my work", "is this done", "did that work", "have a
look", "ready to ship?", and the end of any do-task run. Reach for it on evidence work
too, where there is no diff to read and the question is whether the act is proven. Not
for judging prose or a document's look, and not for opening a change request.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-artifacts: Gates the tooling an agent reads — skills, commands, rules, CLAUDE.md — asking whether
the file has one clear job, delivers it end to end, leaves the choices the project owns
to the project, matches the repo as it actually is, and can be followed without guessing.
Returns PASS, REVISE or CUT. CUT is the verdict nothing else makes: this artifact
duplicates another or does nothing, and should be removed. - Use whenever a file an agent reads is written or changed — a SKILL.md, a slash command, a
rules file, CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md — and before adding a new one to a collection, since
the overlap question is easiest to answer while it is still cheap. Also on request:
"review this skill", "is this command any good", "does this rule earn its place", "why
isn't my skill triggering", "do we need both of these". Judges whether the artifact does
its job; the look and the words of a human-read document are a different review.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-phrasing: Reviews the words of a document a person will read, and returns PASS or REVISE. Starts
by establishing what the file actually is and who reads it, because a markdown file
carries no contract the way a source file does, and the same wording is correct in a
talk track and wrong in a test case. Then runs check-prose.sh to locate the mechanical
tells by grep rather than by impression, and judges what a pattern cannot reach. - Use whenever prose a person will read is written or edited: a README, a design doc or
RFC, a test plan, a QA report, a bug report, API or CLI reference, release notes, slide
content, a demo script. Also on request: "does this read okay", "make this clearer",
"tighten this up", "write this up", "too wordy". Reach for it on a document that is
factually correct and still hard to read, and on any document an agent generated, which
is the case that most needs it and least asks for it.

- agent-workflows:reviewing-typography: Reviews how a human-read document looks — a README, prose and tables in docs/, an HTML
page — and returns PASS or REVISE. Works the way a UI designer does: group the content,
space the groups so the inner gap is smaller than the outer one, emphasize by dimming
what is not the point rather than shouting what is, hold the level count low, and judge
the page whole rather than section by section. Judges the look; the words are a separate
review. - Use whenever a document a person will read is written or restructured — a README, a
guide, release notes, an HTML page — and before it reaches its reader. Also on request:
"does this read okay", "make this scannable", "why does this look like a wall", "clean
up the formatting", "too many headings". Reach for it on a doc that is factually right
and still hard to get through, which is the case nobody thinks to ask about.

- agent-workflows:take-issue: Picks up a tracked issue of any kind and claims it: resolves which one, reads it whole
along with the log it links, judges whether it can actually be started, and refuses it
back when it cannot. Assigns it, moves the state label, cuts a branch where a diff is
coming, and stops before any work begins — so a misreading is catchable while it is still
cheap. The read half of an issue; something else does the work. - Use whenever work is about to start on something already tracked, whatever kind it is —
"work on #42", "what's next", "pick something up", "grab the next one", "I'll take that",
"what should I do now". Code: "start on the parser bug". Docs: "fix that README issue".
Environment: "do the staging upgrade". Operations: "rotate that cert", "run the
migration", "take the cert one". Reach for it before any work begins, not only before
code — an operation issue is claimed the same way and is the case most likely to be
started without ever being picked up. Reach for it even when the issue number is known
and the work looks obvious, because the point is to read the issue rather than to
remember it. Not for filing something new, and not for doing the work once claimed.

- mattpocock-skills:diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
